newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Arafat says West Bank settlements "very serious".
newsitem.headline: Arafat says West Bank settlements "very serious".

text.p: Palestinian President Yasser Arafat said on Tuesday that expansion of Israeli settlements in occupied Arab lands was in clear breach of U.S.-sponsored peace accords.
"These settlements are a very serious event. This is a clear breach (of) what has been agreed upon," Arafat told Austrian state television in an interview during a two-day official visit to Vienna.

"(They are) a clear and obvious contradiction to the guarantee which has been offered to us by (former U.S. Secretary of State James) Baker in which they mentioned there would be no geographic changes in the transition during the talks," Arafat added, according to a translation of his remarks.
He said a failure of Israeli-Palestinian talks on an Israeli troop pullback in the West Bank town of Hebron could throw the entire region into confusion and chaos.
"That would mean there will be very difficult circumstances in the whole area. You can't imagine what can come out of this confusion," he said.

Talks between the two sides on the Hebron issue have ground to a deadlock over security arrangements for the 400 Jews in the heart of Hebron living amid more than 100,000 Arabs. Hebron is the last of seven West Bank towns from which Israeli troops are supposed to redeploy.
According to a 1995 deal signed in Washington by Arafat and late Israeli Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin, Israel is due to hand over 80 percent of Hebron to Palestinian rule.
Palestinians accuse Netanyahu of trying to renege on the peace deal signed by his Labour party predecessor.

Hopes for a speedy conclusion of the negotiations were stoked earlier on Tuesday when Austrian Chancellor Franz Vranitzky said Nentanyahu had told him over the phone a deal on Hebron could be expected within days.

The United States, sponsor of Arab-Israeli peace talks since they were launched in 1991, has voiced increasing impatience with the Middle East deadlock, following a sharp attack on Monday by U.S. President Bill Clinton on Isreal's policy of promoting Jewish settlements in the West Bank.
Arafat reiterated that the Palestinians were fully commitment to continuing the peace process.

"Not only Palestinians need the peace. The Israelis, the Arabs, the world needs the peace," he said. "What we are asking for is the exact and honest implementation of what we have agreed upon. We are not asking for the moon."
